Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for accessing public healthcare services
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced a clearly relevant authoritative picture, so this was moved from fast path to full verification. Burundi's biometric national digital ID was only unveiled in May 2026 and is not yet operational (awaiting enabling legislation and a nationwide issuance calendar), so it cannot currently function as a healthcare-access credential. Public healthcare/health-insurance access is instead managed via the separate Carte d'Assistance Maladie (CAM), made compulsory by ordinance in February 2025 for adults without other coverage; a 2023 World Bank digital-health study also notes the lack of a unified digital identifier linking health records. No source found in which the national ID (digital or paper) is described as accepted or required for healthcare access. Recalculated from 0/Unknown to 1/No.
revised_comments: Burundi's national digital identity system was unveiled in May 2026 but remains pre-operational, pending adoption of its enabling legal framework and a nationwide issuance timetable. Access to public healthcare services is instead governed through the Carte d'Assistance Maladie (CAM), a separate health-insurance card that became compulsory in February 2025 for adults not otherwise covered. There is no evidence that the national identity credential is accepted or required for healthcare access; a 2023 World Bank study on digital health in Burundi further notes the absence of a unified digital identifier linking patients across the health system.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for registering for social assistance programs and accessing social services
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced clearly relevant World Bank project documentation, so this was moved from fast path to full verification. The World Bank-financed safety-net project design (PAD, 2016) states that national ID cards are required for the mobile-money registration used to pay cash-transfer beneficiaries, and that where recipients lack an ID the project supports them to obtain one and may issue a temporary programme card in the interim. A July 2025 World Bank policy note confirms the current Cash for Jobs/Merankabandi programme (active since 2022, ~1.25 million beneficiaries nationally) still pays via mobile money, consistent with continued reliance on the ID credential for registration. No source states registration is impossible without an ID, so this is 'accepted but not mandatory' rather than strictly mandatory. Recalculated from 0/Unknown to 2/Accepted but not mandatory.
revised_comments: Burundi's flagship social protection programme, the World Bank-financed Cash for Jobs project (Merankabandi), which reaches around 1.25 million beneficiaries nationally, pays transfers via mobile money and requires beneficiaries to hold a national identity card to register for the mobile line used for payment. Where a household lacks an identity card, the programme supports the individual to obtain one and can issue a temporary programme card to allow initial payments to proceed, so the credential is used in registration but is not a strict precondition for enrolment.
